idiom_name: feature detection: typeof x.flush === 'function' / 'flush' in x, plus well-known-symbol protocols
implementation_notes: With no type system and no interfaces, the JavaScript query is a property test on the object itself: `typeof x.flush === 'function'` (or `'flush' in x`) asks whether the capability is present, and the caller invokes it only when the answer is yes - the idiom the web platform calls feature detection, used at object level ('flush' in writer) and at environment level (typeof window.fetch === 'function'). Capability protocols are standardised as well-known symbols, so the same question is spelled `typeof x[Symbol.iterator] === 'function'` for iteration and `typeof x[Symbol.asyncIterator] === 'function'` for async iteration, and a class can answer `x instanceof Iterable` structurally by defining a static Symbol.hasInstance that tests for the protocol instead of the prototype chain. What replaces the classic structure is this duck-typing protocol; an explicit interface description (a JSDoc typedef or a published TypeScript declaration) is justified only when the capability is a contract for other developers.
pitfalls: A present method is not a working one: stubs that throw 'not implemented', platform-conditional methods and proxies all pass the presence test, so the call path still needs its own error handling.
Presence checks test a name, not a signature or a brand; a property of the wrong type passes 'in', and typeof reports 'function' for classes as well as functions.
instanceof walks the prototype chain, so it fails across realms (iframes, workers) and for structurally valid objects; prefer feature detection or a Symbol.hasInstance brand.
Symbol.hasInstance replaces the semantics of instanceof for the whole class, so a buggy brand test breaks every consumer of that operator.
